messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Julian Vance was twenty-four when the relationship that had promised stability devolved into a controlled cycle of violence. It began with slammed doors and escalated to blows that left his ribs bruised and his jaw split open. His partner always came home reeking of whiskey, the sour scent clinging to his clothes before the shouting began. Julian learned to brace himself, but the violence sometimes arrived without warning, leaving him slumped against the wall, watching his own blood soak into the floor. The first time Julian felt a wave of nausea roll through his gut, it was right as a punch connected with his cheek; now, that same sickening lurch was a phantom echo of the impact. Over the following months, Julian braced whenever he caught the whiff of liquor at a block party. The smell of alcohol didn’t just remind him of his ex; it pulled the memory of his bruised ribs and split jaw into his mind with violent immediacy. That sensory spike confirmed his growing certainty that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that people could not be trusted. He had come to believe that every stranger’s hands were potential threats, his faith in life’s inherent fairness eroding with each unprovoked strike. What frightened him most was the realization that his own body had become a map of his past violence. The memories refused to fade, replaying the assaults with brutal clarity: the scuff of boots on hardwood, the crack of bone against wood, the flickering streetlamp before the next blow landed. They forced their way into his thoughts during quiet moments, hijacking his focus with unbidden auditory echoes—the slap of a belt buckle, the wet thud against drywall—that made his breath catch. Faced with this internal siege, Julian adopted rigid habits to keep the pain at bay. He refused to relax, convinced that letting his guard down guaranteed he would be caught off guard again. He wrapped his emotions in thick cotton, deliberately dulling his feelings to avoid processing the terror. He also stopped allowing anyone near him; his wife’s attempts to hold his hand met with stiff withdrawals, his body recoiling from touch as if anticipating a strike. As these avoidance strategies accumulated over months, they reshaped his reality. He was certain that numbing was the only way to function, but it only reinforced his belief that he was permanently disconnected from everyone else, an outsider watching life through glass. This suspicion of hidden motives didn’t just color his present; it actively sharpened his memories, turning ordinary recollections into visceral warnings. His refusal to relax and habit of emotional numbing left his nervous system perpetually braced, meaning that when a colleague’s sudden movement crossed his path, his body immediately spiked with familiar nausea. Every time he pushed away his wife or refused to unwind, the distance between him and the present grew, and the past memories pressed against his consciousness with renewed force. When he finally sat in his patrol car after a domestic violence call, the victim’s swollen eye and the faint whiff of bourbon triggered that violent, uncontrolled nausea. Julian gripped the wheel, unable to reconcile the badge on his chest with the trembling man who had spent months surviving by never letting his guard down. The cycle outpaced his coping mechanisms. Julian was seeking help not to relive the abuse, but because carrying it alone was fracturing his marriage and threatening his career. He feared that without intervention, the memories would continue to dictate his every move, leaving him isolated and convinced that danger was everywhere. What he hoped for, quietly and desperately, was a way to unclench his stomach, sit still without scanning for exits, and believe that not every hand reaching for him was meant to strike.
